In a one-dimensional array, a peak is defined by a local property [1]. Specifically, a position is a peak if it is greater than or equal to its neighbors [1][7]. 

For example, in an array where positions are represented by letters $a$ through $i$, position $b$ is a peak if and only if $b \geq a$ and $b \geq c$ [1][7]. At the edges of the array, you only need to look to one side; for instance, if position $i$ is at the far right, it is a peak if $i \geq h$ [3][7].

An array will always have a peak if the definition of a peak uses "greater than or equal to" ($\ge$) [1]. If the definition is changed to "greater than" ($>$), the argument that a peak always exists does not hold [1].

The worst-case running time of the straightforward algorithm that starts from the left and walks across the array is $\Theta(n)$ [1, 6]. This algorithm might touch all of the elements in the worst case [4, 6].

To find a peak in a 1D array using divide and conquer, the algorithm follows these steps:

*   **Check the middle element:** Look at the position $n/2$ and compare it to its neighbors [5, 9].
*   **Determine direction:**
    *   If $a[n/2] < a[n/2 - 1]$, the algorithm only looks at the left half of the array ($1 \dots n/2 - 1$) to find a peak [5, 9].
    *   Else if $a[n/2] < a[n/2 + 1]$, the algorithm only looks at the right half of the array ($n/2 + 1 \dots n$) to find a peak [5, 9].
    *   Otherwise, the $n/2$ position is a peak [5, 9].

The complexity of this algorithm is $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(1) + \dots + \Theta(1)$ ($\log_2(n)$ times), which results in a complexity of $\Theta(\log_2(n))$ [5, 9]. The $\Theta(1)$ term represents the work required to compare $a[n/2]$ to its neighbors [5, 9].

The time complexity of the 1D divide and conquer peak finder is $\Theta(\log_2 n)$ [1].

This complexity is derived from the recurrence relation $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(1) + \dots + \Theta(1)$ performed $\log_2(n)$ times [1]. The algorithm works by comparing an element at $a[n/2]$ to its neighbors to determine which half of the array to search next [1].

An element at position $(i, j)$ is a 2D peak if it is greater than or equal to its adjacent elements [2][8]. Specifically, $(i, j)$ is a 2D peak if:

*   It is the maximum element in its column, meaning it is greater than or equal to the elements above and below it [2].
*   It is greater than or equal to the elements to its left $(i, j-1)$ and to its right $(i, j+1)$ [2][8].

If neither the left nor the right condition triggers (meaning the element is greater than or equal to both neighbors), then the element is a 2D peak [2][8].
The greedy ascent algorithm for 2D peak finding has a worst-case complexity of $\Theta(nm)$ [1, 2, 9]. In the specific case where $n = m$, the complexity is $\Theta(n^2)$ [1, 2, 9].

Finding a 1D peak in the middle column does not guarantee a 2D peak because a 1D peak on a row may not be a 2D peak [3, 4]. 

In an attempt to extend 1D Divide and Conquer to 2D, one might pick a middle column $j = m/2$, find a 1D-peak at $(i, j)$, and then use $(i, j)$ as a starting point to find a 1D-peak on row $i$ [3]. However, this approach fails because the resulting 1D-peak on that row might not satisfy the conditions to be a 2D peak [3, 4]. For example, in a $4 \times 4$ grid, a value of 14 can be a 1D-peak on its row but fail to be a 2D peak [4].

The running time of the 2D peak algorithm that picks the middle column and finds its global maximum is $\Theta(n \log m)$ [3][8]. If the matrix is square such that $m = n$, the complexity is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [3][8].

The complexity is derived from the following recurrence relation:
$T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + \Theta(n)$ [3][8]

In this recurrence, $\Theta(n)$ represents the work required to find the global maximum on a column of $n$ rows [3][8]. This results in the total work being the sum of $\log m$ instances of $\Theta(n)$ [3][8].

The word "algorithm" comes from Al-Khwarizmi (also spelled Al-Khwarazmi), who is considered the "father of algebra" [3][4]. He wrote a book titled *The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing* [3][4]. His work, which involved solving linear and quadratic equations, is associated with the origins of the word [1][3].

The Random Access Machine (RAM) is a mathematical analog of a real random access memory [1]. It is modeled as a large array consisting of $\Theta(1)$ registers, where each register holds one word [2].

Key characteristics of the RAM model include:
*   **Structure:** The memory is organized by words at specific addresses, such as address 0, address 1, and so on [4]. A diagram of this model illustrates memory as a vertical stack of rectangular cells indexed from $0$ to $5$ [7].
*   **Operations:** In $\Theta(1)$ time, the model can perform the following operations:
    *   Load a word from memory at address $r_i$ into register $r_j$ [3].
    *   Compute operations on registers using $(+, -, *, /, \&, |, \wedge)$ [3].
    *   Store a register $r_j$ into memory at address $r_i$ [3].
*   **Word Size:** A word $w$ is defined such that $w \geq \lg(\text{memory size})$ bits [3]. It is assumed that basic objects, such as integers, fit within a word [3].
*   **Purpose:** The RAM is a realistic and powerful model used to implement abstractions [3]. While the RAM and pointer machine are theoretical models designed to be simple so that operations take constant time, the RAM specifically provides a way to structure thinking about algorithms [1, 5].

A pointer machine is a model of computation consisting of dynamically allocated objects [1, 5]. In this model, each object has a constant number of fields, denoted as $O(1)$ [2, 5]. A field can be either a "word" (such as an integer) or a pointer to another object or a null value (also known as nil or none) [1, 5].

Key characteristics of the pointer machine include:
* **Manipulation:** Manipulating an object is considered to take constant time, provided the object has a constant number of attributes [2].
* **Implementation:** The pointer machine is a weaker model than the Random Access Machine (RAM) because it can be implemented on a RAM [5]. In a RAM implementation, a pointer becomes an index into a large table [4].
* **Structure:** An example of a structure in a pointer machine is a linked list, where nodes contain fields such as pointers to the previous and next elements, as well as a value [3].
* **Terminology:** While the model is called a pointer machine, the pointers in this model are actually references [3]. Modern languages often use the term "references" because "pointers" can be perceived as "scary" [1, 3].

Appending an item to a Python list, represented as `L.append(x)`, takes $\theta(1)$ time [4][9]. While the obvious way to increase an array's size is to allocate a new array and copy all elements—which would take linear time—Python does not do that [1]. Instead, the operation is $\theta(1)$ [4].

The distance between two documents is defined by treating each document as a vector where each component $D[w]$ represents the number of occurrences of a specific word $W$ in that document [2, 3, 9].

To compute the distance, the following process is used:
*   **Vector Representation:** A document is viewed as a giant vector of word frequencies [2]. For example, if $D_1 = \text{"the cat"}$ and $D_2 = \text{"the dog"}$, they are represented as vectors in a coordinate system where axes correspond to words like "dog", "the", and "cat" [7].
*   **Normalization:** A simple dot product is not scale invariant, meaning long documents with many shared words might incorrectly seem farther apart than short documents with fewer shared words [1]. To fix this, the dot product is normalized by the number of words in the documents [1]. This is expressed as:
    $$d''(D_1, D_2) = \frac{D_1 \cdot D_2}{|D_1| \cdot |D_2|}$$ [7]
*   **Angle Calculation:** The final document distance $d(D_1, D_2)$ is defined as the angle between the two vectors [1, 4]:
    $$d(D_1, D_2) = \arccos(d''(D_1, D_2))$$ [1, 7]

An angle of $0^\circ$ indicates the two documents are identical, while an angle of $90^\circ$ indicates there are no common words between them [1, 4, 7].

Insertion sort works by iterating through an input array and inserting each element into its correct position within a previously sorted sub-array [1, 4, 7]. 

The process follows these steps:
*   **Iteration:** The algorithm iterates from $j = 2$ to $n$ [4, 7, 8].
*   **Insertion:** For each index $j$, the algorithm takes the element $A[j]$ (the "key") and inserts it into the already sorted sub-array $A[1 \dots j-1]$ [4, 7].
*   **Positioning:** This insertion is achieved by performing pairwise key-swaps to move the element down to its correct position [1, 4, 7].

An example of this process on the array $[8, 2, 4, 9, 3, 6]$ shows the following steps:
1.  The number $2$ is moved before $8$ to result in $[2, 8, 4, 9, 3, 6]$ [3].
2.  The number $4$ is moved before $8$ to result in $[2, 4, 8, 9, 3, 6]$ [3].
3.  The number $9$ stays in its current position [3].
4.  The number $3$ is moved before $4$ to result in $[2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 6]$ [3].
5.  The number $6$ is moved before $8$ to result in $[2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9]$ [3].

Using binary search within insertion sort reduces the number of comparisons to $\Theta(n \log n)$ [1], but it does not improve the overall worst-case complexity because of the cost of shifting elements [2][3].

Specifically:
*   **Comparisons:** Binary search can find the correct position for an element in $\Theta(\log i)$ time because the sub-array $A[0 \dots i-1]$ is already sorted [3]. This results in $\Theta(n \log n)$ comparisons [1].
*   **Swaps/Shifts:** Even if the correct position is found quickly, if you are using an array data structure, you must shift the elements after the insertion point to the right to make room [2][3]. In the worst case, shifting these elements takes $\Theta(n)$ time [2].
*   **Overall Complexity:** Because of these necessary shifts, the algorithm still has a $\Theta(n^2)$ complexity when looking at swaps [1][2][5].

The merge step in merge sort uses a "two-finger algorithm" to combine two sorted arrays into a single sorted array [7]. This routine works by interspersing or interleaving the elements from the two arrays [7].

The process involves the following:
*   **Pointer Movement**: The algorithm uses pointers to walk up the two arrays [4]. In the example provided, the smallest remaining element from the bottom of either array is selected and placed into the merged output sequence [1].
*   **Selection**: As the algorithm progresses, it compares elements and selects the appropriate one to write down [4]. For instance, if one element is smaller than the other, that element is written down, and the pointer for that array moves to the next element [4].
*   **Complexity**: When merging two arrays of size $n/2$, the complexity of this routine is $\Theta(n)$ [5][7]. All of the actual work of the merge sort algorithm is performed during this merge routine [4][6].
Merge sort requires $\Theta(n)$ auxiliary space [2]. This extra space is needed to take the results from the recursive sorting steps and put them into the sorted array $A$ [2].

The running time of merge sort is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [3, 6].

You can see this through the following methods:

*   **Recurrence Relation:** The algorithm follows a divide and conquer structure where the work is defined by the recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn$, where $c > 0$ is a constant [2, 6]. This recurrence accounts for the two recursive calls to sort the halves of the array and the $\Theta(n)$ time required to merge the two sorted lists [2, 6].
*   **Recursion Tree:** Using a recursion tree, it can be observed that there is an equal amount of work done at each level of the tree [4, 6]. The total work is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [6].
*   **Proof by Picture:** An intuitive way to understand the result is through a "proof by picture," which helps provide intuition behind why the result is true before formalizing it [3].
